Murder on the Orient Express. Agatha Christie's 1934 novel features detective Hercule Poirot aboard a snowbound luxury train where a wealthy American is found murdered in his locked cabin. With no escape possible and a train full of suspects, Poirot must unravel a murder with multiple motives and solve a puzzle of extraordinary complexity.

An American businessman, Samuel Ratchett—actually a criminal in hiding—is murdered in a locked compartment aboard the Orient Express. The train becomes snowbound in the Balkans, trapping all suspects on board with no possibility of escape or outside interference. Poirot examines each of the twelve suspects and discovers that all have plausible motives and opportunities for the murder.

As the investigation deepens, it reveals that Ratchett was involved in a kidnapping and murder years prior, for which he was never punished. Poirot deduces that all twelve suspects conspired together to murder Ratchett, each striking a blow in revenge for the victim they knew. The solution is a democratic murder: a conspiracy of justice rather than an individual crime. It exemplifies the closed room mystery expanded to an entire train.

When faced with this extraordinary puzzle and a profound moral dilemma about justice itself, Poirot presents multiple possible solutions to the Turkish police and train officials, allowing them to accept the most convenient lie. One of Christie's most famous and celebrated novels, it remains a masterpiece of multiple suspects and systematic elimination.
